analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps to $6.65 an hour.
analysis.headline: A bill to raise the minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.65 an hour won support from 37 senators — all Democrats — but the Senate never voted on it, and it expired with the 107th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the federal wage floor in three steps: $5.75 an hour 30 days after enactment, $6.25 in 2002, and $6.65 starting January 1, 2003 [S3]. It would also, for the first time, apply the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, phasing that wage in over several years [S3]. The bill was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, where it sat with no committee action and no floor vote before the Congress ended [S1].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, who would see hourly pay rise from $5.15 to as much as $6.65 by 2003 [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps — $5.75 within 30 days of passage, $6.25 in 2002, and $6.65 on January 1, 2003 — from the $5.15 floor in place since 1997.
Extends the federal minimum wage to the Northern Mariana Islands, which had been exempt, starting at $3.55 and rising 50 cents every six months until it reaches the federal floor.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum-wage workers — concentrated in restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service businesses — through higher payroll costs, some of which may be passed to consumers.

drawbacks.text: Employers would bear higher per-hour labor costs, and the increase falls hardest on small businesses and industries like food service where minimum-wage pay is most common; economists continue to debate how much such increases reduce entry-level hiring.

The bill contained no tax breaks or credits to offset the cost for small employers — a contrast with competing Republican proposals that paired a smaller wage increase with business tax relief, which opponents cited as reason to oppose it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a straightforward, sizable raise for the lowest-paid workers, phased in over about two years, with the cost borne by their employers and spread among consumers. The main honest objections are the burden on small businesses and the contested employment effects of a wage floor; the bill was a simple increase with no offsets, which made it cleaner for workers but easier for opponents to paint as a cost mandate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate's calendar of bills awaiting floor action, but nobody ever called it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on May 25, 2001, joined by 24 other Democratic senators as original sponsors.
The next day it was read a second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders — Calendar No. 54 — the list of bills waiting to be brought to the floor.
No committee was assigned, no floor debate was scheduled, and no vote ever occurred; the bill's action history ends there for the entire two-year Congress.
The bill had 37 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat, in a Senate with 49 Democratic seats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers, who kept the $5.15 floor for another Congress, and the Bush administration, which had proposed a smaller increase tied to business tax cuts rather than this standalone raise.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 24 fellow Democrats as original sponsors.

for.name: 37 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from every Senate Democrat who signed on but no Republican.

for.name: Senate Democratic leadership
for.role: Held the Senate majority in the 107th Congress and controlled which calendar bills reached the floor
for.what_they_did: Never brought S. 964 up for floor debate or a vote despite it sitting on the calendar and being sponsored by their own leader; the majority's attention went to other priorities, including the September 11 response.

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None signed on to the bill; Republicans favored a smaller increase paired with business tax breaks and had enough seats to filibuster a standalone raise.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the 37 cosponsors was a Democrat and no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, though the record shows no recorded vote on either side.

industries.note: Restaurants are the largest employer of minimum-wage workers, so a higher wage floor directly raises their labor costs; their interest in blocking the bill ran against the workers who would have gotten the raise.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Retail, lodging, and similar businesses pay many entry-level wages at the federal floor and would have absorbed the higher mandated pay, with some costs passed to customers.

industries.industry: Northern Mariana Islands garment and tourism industries
industries.note: The islands had been exempt from the federal minimum wage, letting local garment factories pay well below it; the bill would have phased the federal floor in there, ending that cost advantage.
